title: Foreign Relations, 1977–1980, Volume III, Foreign Economic Policy
intro: Use the Carter foreign economic policy volume as an editorial model for explaining U.S. choices about the international economic system. The current emphasis is on financial institutions: their resources, lending rules, governance, and the U.S. decisions that shaped them.
adaptation: These are working editorial judgments for the Bush compilation. The Carter examples illustrate selection and annotation methods; they are not evidence for events in 1989–1992. The Bush proposals retain one continuous chronology and their own first-page NARA PDF provenance.

principles.title: Select a consequential choice
principles.text: Ask what options were available, who advocated them, what was at stake, and what the President or responsible principal decided. A Scowcroft memorandum merits space when it explains that process.

principles.title: Read across the economic agencies
principles.text: Pursue Treasury, State, USTR, CEA, OMB, and, for monetary issues, Federal Reserve and U.S. executive-director records alongside NSC papers. Compare the responsible agency’s case with Scowcroft’s advice.

principles.title: Connect advice to negotiation and disposition
principles.text: Build a sequence from the originating proposal through interagency disagreement, instructions, and a record of bargaining or disposition. Use annotation to connect supporting papers and public outcomes; identify a missing meeting record or unmarked decision explicitly.

principles.title: Keep the institutional question in view
principles.text: Select country-specific material when it explains a wider lending rule, voting precedent, debt strategy, or division of responsibility. Use clearly marked extracts where the rest belongs in a regional volume. Preserve the broader monetary, trade, summit, and development-policy remit.

examples.label: Bonn summit minutes
examples.lesson: The minutes preserve exchanges among leaders about monetary arrangements. The edition marks omissions and routes the energy discussion to the energy volume.
examples.application: For Paris and Houston, pair briefing papers with the actual economic discussions and identify the institutional passages to retain.

examples.label: Strauss to Carter: Tokyo Round assessment
examples.lesson: A trade negotiator explains the bargain abroad and the coalition needed for congressional approval at home.
examples.application: Seek equivalent Uruguay Round choices, including agriculture, subsidies, concessions, and domestic authority; summit references alone do not complete the trade record.

examples.label: Miller: proposed IMF substitution account
examples.lesson: The paper specifies U.S. exposure, safeguards, and negotiating conditions. Annotation reports that no meeting record was found and follows the proposal to suspension.
examples.application: For IMF quotas and EBRD design, retain financial terms and political authority; distinguish a recommended position from a concluded agreement.

examples.label: Bergsten to Blumenthal: IDA V negotiations
examples.lesson: A Treasury negotiating report connects donor commitments to congressional appropriations. Notes supply the earlier instructions and later agreement.
examples.application: For IDA, IMF resources, and the Multilateral Investment Fund, trace pledges, appropriations, other donors’ conditions, and the eventual disposition.

examples.label: Christopher to Carter: IFI voting and human rights
examples.lesson: An extract isolates the institutional voting issue from an evening report. Annotation records presidential marginalia and the subsequent legislative result.
examples.application: For China, Brazil, and the Philippines, make the general lending or voting principle explicit and retain omission markers in any proposed extract.

examples.label: PRC conclusions on North–South strategy
examples.lesson: The record identifies participants, policy questions, conclusions, and assigned work. Its source note separately establishes presidential approval of the summary.
examples.application: For U.S. loan-review procedures, look for agreed instructions and later adjudication; an administrative meeting arrangement is supporting evidence.

examples.label: Blumenthal to Carter: development-bank strategy
examples.lesson: A Treasury decision paper compares IDA, IBRD, and IDB commitments, State’s alternative, and budget costs. Editorial notes state where Carter left recommendations unmarked.
examples.application: Favor papers that connect institutions and explain alternatives, funding, and U.S. influence. Blank approval lines must remain unresolved.

researchPriorities.title: Complete the institutional decision sequences
researchPriorities.text: Find Treasury instructions, executive-director positions, board votes, and signed presidential or principals’ dispositions for the IMF, EBRD, and development-bank episodes already proposed. These are follow-up targets, not additional verified selections.

researchPriorities.title: Compare the financial agencies’ own records
researchPriorities.text: Use Scowcroft’s files to locate disagreements, then seek the originating Treasury and State analyses and relevant OMB, CEA, Federal Reserve, or executive-director material. Do not infer that a parallel record exists or is released.

researchPriorities.title: Give trade and monetary policy their own decision records
researchPriorities.text: Extend the current institution-heavy proposal set with verified papers on Uruguay Round negotiating choices, exchange-rate coordination, and international monetary arrangements. Retain the project’s established cross-volume routing for Canada and Mexico.

researchPriorities.title: Connect debt and development to system-wide policy
researchPriorities.text: Seek choices over concessional resources, creditor burden-sharing, development-bank mandates, and commodity mechanisms where the Bush record establishes their importance. A counterpart to every Carter topic is not required.

assessments.assessment: Retain the NSC assessment if it adds policy judgment beyond the underlying Sherpa report; otherwise use it to annotate that fuller record.
assessments.followUp: Compare McCormack’s report with the U.S. instructions and the subsequent summit discussion.

assessments.assessment: Use the action copy to explain preparation and routing of the March 20 paper. Meeting organization alone is insufficient for a separate policy document.
assessments.followUp: Locate the substantive discussion or conclusions of the proposed White House Summit Group meeting.

assessments.assessment: Select if the allocation of authority materially explains how summit objectives were settled; pair it with the substantive objectives.
assessments.followUp: Find the principals’ discussion and the President’s guidance for the next Sherpa meeting.

assessments.assessment: The selection value lies in the proposed NSC role in trade strategy and the reason for it. Establish the recommendation before describing any resulting directive.
assessments.followUp: Find the signed or sent reply and the economic-policy directive or review record to which it responded.

assessments.assessment: Annotate the preparation of the June 24 briefing; avoid giving staff routing the same weight as presidential objectives.
assessments.followUp: Find a record of the June 26 briefing and subsequent Paris bargaining.

assessments.assessment: A strong statement of U.S. objectives across monetary coordination, debt, and trade. Preserve the relationships among those choices.
assessments.followUp: Compare with Treasury and State instructions, presidential guidance, and the summit conversation record.

assessments.assessment: Use the joint State–Treasury assessment to establish the agencies’ proposed bargain, then compare Scowcroft’s response.
assessments.followUp: Find summit exchanges and subsequent instructions that establish which proposed positions became U.S. policy.

assessments.assessment: Use for the association and timing of the undated China-lending attachment. The cover cannot supply a signed presidential decision.
assessments.followUp: Seek a controlling signed or annotated copy and the resulting U.S. voting instructions.

assessments.assessment: Use to reconstruct the briefing packet and distinguish its substantive attachments; count each attachment once.
assessments.followUp: Compare the President’s briefing-book copy and the actual Houston discussions.

assessments.assessment: Select for the interaction of World Bank lending policy, G-7 coordination, and U.S. legal constraints. The blank decision lines remain unresolved.
assessments.followUp: Locate the presidential disposition and U.S. board instructions; coordinate any China-specific narrative with the regional volume.

assessments.assessment: Select the distinct NSC judgment on the multilateral economic bargain, especially agriculture and assistance conditions; assess regional passages for cross-volume treatment.
assessments.followUp: Compare Baker–Brady’s recommendations with summit discussions and the agreed economic text.

assessments.assessment: Use as an opening statement of U.S. preferences on Fund resources, debt guarantees, and surveillance. It shows proposed resistance and alternatives before the strategy matured.
assessments.followUp: Find Treasury’s position and the instructions or decisions adopted after this recommendation.

assessments.assessment: Useful for the early institutional choices. Compare with the January 9 briefing and January 16 report before deciding how much preliminary explanation requires full text.
assessments.followUp: Identify which membership, capital, and lending conditions entered the U.S. negotiating instructions.

assessments.assessment: Retain the proposed eligibility and mandate rules if they establish the position taken into negotiations; use overlapping background in annotation.
assessments.followUp: Compare the principals’ conclusions and the delegation’s instructions with the January 16 negotiating report.

assessments.assessment: A strong link between proposed policy and agreed instructions. Preserve the distinction between Deal’s report of conclusions and any separately approved meeting record.
assessments.followUp: Seek the underlying conclusions or implementing instructions on World Bank China loans and EBRD participation.

assessments.assessment: A strong candidate because the negotiating team reports concrete obstacles and disagreements over institutional design.
assessments.followUp: Compare with the agreed U.S. instructions and the later terms recommended to the President.

assessments.assessment: Retain if Deal’s assessment explains a consequential choice between participation and withdrawal that is not adequately captured in the joint report.
assessments.followUp: Find the principals’ response; compare the January 16 report to avoid repeating its negotiation narrative.

assessments.assessment: Propose an institutional-policy extract if the released passages add distinctive choices on the EBRD, IMF, or World Bank. Preserve redactions and identify omitted unrelated material.
assessments.followUp: Find conclusions of the breakfast and fuller released copies of the relevant institutional papers.

assessments.assessment: The currency-denomination and financial-exposure problem gives this paper broader significance than a routine progress report.
assessments.followUp: Trace the approval to inform Mulford into the instructions sent and the final capital arrangements.

assessments.assessment: A strong decision-stage paper: Scowcroft recommends joining and specifies governance and lending terms. It remains a briefing, not minutes of the meeting.
assessments.followUp: Find the President’s disposition and compare the charter and U.S. participation authority with the recommended terms.

assessments.assessment: Use the changed lending and membership terms to document movement toward agreement. Consider annotation if a later report captures these changes and their causes more fully.
assessments.followUp: Locate resolution of the remaining capital, shareholding, board, and leadership questions.

assessments.assessment: Select the institutional passages on arrears, conditionality, and EBRD governance; their value is the relationship between financial rules and diplomatic priorities.
assessments.followUp: Find the principals’ conclusions and subsequent IMF, World Bank, or IDB action; mark any omitted bilateral material.

assessments.assessment: Select for the allocation of debt-reduction costs between commercial creditors and multilateral institutions. Country cases should illustrate that general strategy.
assessments.followUp: Compare Treasury’s Brady-strategy instructions with the relevant institutional financing decisions.

assessments.assessment: Useful if it explains why a new donor mechanism was disputed and how it would relate to existing institutions. Compare later, fuller assessments for annotation alternatives.
assessments.followUp: Find State’s proposed design, Treasury’s response, and a decision on the donor mechanism.

assessments.assessment: The choice between a new fund and existing IDB/AID programs is the institutional question to retain, together with its resource implications.
assessments.followUp: Locate the President’s response and the ensuing U.S. position on the proposed fund.

assessments.assessment: Retain the competing institutional designs and donor-funding consequences. This supplies substantive disagreement behind the coordination papers.
assessments.followUp: Seek Treasury and State originals and the agreed division of responsibilities between their initiatives.

assessments.assessment: Select for the allocation of scarce U.S. and donor resources if it explains a consequential funding choice; distinguish the marked action from later commitments.
assessments.followUp: Trace the approved staff action into OMB clearance, donor commitments, and the final funding arrangement.

assessments.assessment: Propose the identified paragraphs as an extract on collective lending pressure and donor coordination. Retain enough context to explain the policy rule.
assessments.followUp: Find the original decision, U.S. board instructions, and subsequent disposition of World Bank and IDB lending.

assessments.assessment: The draft makes the policy and funding case for ESAF. Prefer the decisive internal recommendation or final transmitted report if available, using this draft to document any significant change.
assessments.followUp: Locate the final report and the decision on the U.S. contribution; compare the draft before treating its language as an adopted position.

assessments.assessment: Select if this is the clearest record of the World Bank resource and debt-financing choices put before Bush; read it with Deal’s corrections.
assessments.followUp: Seek the June 21 lunch record and subsequent IDA and debt-financing instructions.

assessments.assessment: Retain the points that alter the President’s understanding of the institutional choices. Consider annotating Porter’s briefing if the corrections can be conveyed concisely.
assessments.followUp: Compare the lunch record, corrected loan information, and the positions actually conveyed to Conable.

assessments.assessment: A strong opening to the loan-vote sequence: a principal identifies the conflict between financial review and foreign-policy consultation.
assessments.followUp: Follow through the alternatives and July 25 instruction, then compare how the appeals process operated.

assessments.assessment: Useful for the actual procedural alternatives considered. If the July 12 assessment adequately preserves them, this paper may serve in annotation.
assessments.followUp: Compare the options with Scowcroft’s July 25 instruction and any agreed operating procedure.

assessments.assessment: A strong analytical companion to the signed instruction because it explains the failure in consultation and the proposed remedy.
assessments.followUp: Compare the final instruction and Treasury’s response, including any change to the proposed appeal route.

assessments.assessment: An anchor for the sequence: it directs advance notice and review of an appeals mechanism. Do not equate the instruction to review arrangements with proof that all resulting procedures were settled.
assessments.followUp: Find the PCC review and resulting procedure, then connect it to the June 1991 Philippine-loan appeal.

assessments.assessment: Select for the distinction between the public bargaining position and the negotiating authority reported in the paper.
assessments.followUp: Compare the outgoing correspondence, Treasury instructions, international agreement, and later U.S. authorization.

assessments.assessment: Use to connect the 1989 process with a concrete appeal. It can annotate the substantive presidential papers if its procedural significance is preserved.
assessments.followUp: Verify how the dispute reached Scowcroft and compare the recommendation, opposing case, and eventual voting instruction.

assessments.assessment: A strong candidate when paired with Baker’s opposing recommendation: the institutional issue is environmental lending standards and their diplomatic cost.
assessments.followUp: Seek a clearly attributable presidential disposition and the resulting U.S. vote; retain the undated dateline and unresolved handwriting.

assessments.assessment: Retain the principal-level alternative so the reader can assess the choice placed before the President, including the comparisons with other lenders.
assessments.followUp: Pair with Scowcroft’s recommendation and locate the presidential response and board outcome.

assessments.assessment: Select if the distinction among quota commitments, authorization, appropriation, and budget outlays explains the administration’s legislative choices.
assessments.followUp: Find Treasury’s legislative strategy, the President’s decisions, and the authorization and appropriation outcome.

assessments.assessment: A strong Treasury intervention linking the U.S. appropriation to other donors’ commitments and competing international priorities.
assessments.followUp: Find Scowcroft’s response, the budget decision, and the conditions under which donor pledges became effective.
